directions: Cape Mendocino reed grass is a compact California native found on windswept coastal bluffs from Mendocino to Sonoma County, forming tight, arching mounds of narrow blue-green foliage. Plant in gritty, fast-draining soil and give it full coastal sun, but provide light afternoon shade and a bit more moisture in hot inland gardens where the coastal fog it evolved with is absent. In early summer, dense purplish flower spikes rise just above the foliage and mature to buff gold, adding fine texture without flopping. Once established it is quite drought tolerant and needs almost no supplemental feeding; simply comb out old foliage in late winter to freshen the clump.

Fontane is a tall selection of purple moor grass named for the fountain-like way its wiry flower stems arch outward from the narrow foliage clump. Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade, where it establishes slowly in the first year or two before settling into a reliable, well-behaved clump. Airy purplish flower panicles appear on tall stems in mid to late summer and hold well without staking, then the whole plant turns a warm golden-amber in fall for one of the best autumn color displays among ornamental grasses. Because the foliage and flower stems die back cleanly and shatter at the base with the first hard frost, cleanup in late winter is simply a matter of pulling away the loosened top growth.

Edith Dudszus is a strictly upright, dark-stemmed selection of purple moor grass, taller than the similar cultivar Moorhexe and blooming somewhat later in the season. Grow it in evenly moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for the darkest stem color, though it also tolerates light shade. The wiry, near-black flower stems rise straight above the low mound of narrow green foliage in late summer, creating a striking vertical accent that contrasts well with mounding or spreading companions. Foliage turns clear gold in autumn before collapsing completely at the first hard freeze, after which the loosened clump can simply be raked clean in late winter ahead of new spring growth.

Tatra Gold is a chartreuse-to-golden-foliaged selection of wavy hair grass that lights up shaded corners where many grasses struggle. Plant in humus-rich, moist but well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in light to dappled shade, since strong afternoon sun can scorch the bright foliage in hot climates. The fine, thread-like leaves form a low, semi-evergreen tuft, and in early summer delicate, airy flower panicles rise on wiry stems well above the foliage, catching light beautifully when backlit. It combines well with ferns, hostas, and other shade perennials, needs little more than an occasional grooming of old leaves, and resents hot, humid summers more than deep cold, so provide extra moisture and afternoon shade in warmer zones.

Pixie Fountain is a compact selection of tufted hair grass, bred for smaller gardens and containers where full-size cultivars would be too large. Plant in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, giving it extra shade and consistent moisture in hot summer regions where the species can struggle. It forms a neat, low tuft of fine green foliage from which airy, shimmering flower panicles rise on slender stems in early summer, often blooming again lightly later in the season if deadheaded. Its small stature makes it useful at the front of a border or in a mixed container, and it needs only an annual combing out of old foliage in late winter to stay tidy.

Sapphire Fountain, also sold under its German name Saphirsprudel, is a selection of blue oat grass chosen for its especially intense steel-blue foliage color and gracefully arching, fountain-like form. Plant in lean to average, sharply drained soil in full sun, since rich soil or excess moisture leads to floppy growth and increases the risk of crown rot, particularly in humid summer climates. The evergreen to semi-evergreen foliage clump holds its blue color best in cooler weather and sends up narrow, oat-like flower spikes on wiry stems in early summer that arch outward above the foliage. It is drought tolerant once established and needs little care beyond an occasional combing to remove dead blades and improve air circulation through the crown.

Lessing's feather grass is a fine-textured steppe grass native to the dry grasslands of Eastern Europe and Central Asia, forming a tight tuft of narrow, silvery-green foliage. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, where it thrives on neglect and is markedly more cold-hardy and long-lived in humid climates than the more commonly grown Mexican feather grass. In late spring to early summer it sends up slender, silky flower plumes that catch the light and move constantly in the slightest breeze, aging from silvery-pink to buff gold by midsummer. It is exceptionally drought tolerant once established and is an excellent choice for xeriscapes, gravel gardens, and rock gardens, needing only a light shearing of old growth in late winter before new leaves emerge.
